title: Read a large biological structure
description: Use MatterViz Pastel and molecular ambient occlusion on 1AON, then inspect chains, cartoons, and an isolated subunit.
text: Get ready Download 1AON.cif and matterviz-pastel.json . 1AON is a deposited GroEL–GroES chaperonin complex. This file imports 58,870 selected atoms , making it a useful example of broad molecular folds and crowded contacts. Read the data source and palette notices . Outcome: an atom-colored space-filling AO view, a chain overview, an isolated protein view, and a PNG of your chosen framing. This is a local graphics workload; allow import and scene preparation to finish before navigating. 1. Prepare the atomic view Click Open and choose 1AON.cif . Wait for the import to finish. Check 58,870 atoms under Molecular data and review Provenance for model, alternate-location, and connection decisions. Set Representation → Van der Waals for space-filling atomic spheres. In Molecular data → Biological structure , set Coloring → Element . This is necessary for the element palette to be visible instead of chain, entity, or secondary-structure colors. Expand Atom colours , click Colours file… , and choose matterviz-pastel.json . Confirm that its filename replaces the built-in palette label. The lighter colors make shaded contacts easier to read. Click Fit scene . Rotate to a useful view of the complex, then leave the camera unchanged for the comparison. Checkpoint: you see atomic spheres colored by element with the Pastel palette. 2. Compare normal lighting and ambient occlusion Under Appearance , leave Ambient occlusion off initially. Observe the contacts and central recesses. Optionally export this view before continuing. Enable Ambient occlusion . Active AO uses Lambert shading plus SSAO , without specular highlights. Keep Automatic AO radius checked and read AO radius (angstrom) . Adjust AO strength while keeping camera, palette, representation, and background unchanged. Compare a moderate strength with zero, then toggle AO off and on. Zero or Off restores normal molecular rendering. For a closer experiment, uncheck Automatic AO radius . The manual slider starts from the automatic value: smaller radii emphasize nearby contacts; larger radii can emphasize broader recesses. Recheck automatic radius afterward. 1AON with normal molecular lighting and AO off. Both captures use the same camera, geometry, MatterViz Pastel palette, Element coloring, Van der Waals representation, and background color #ecebe4 . The matching view with Lambert shading plus SSAO at 100% strength and the automatic 14.25 Å radius. The difference includes the active mode’s matte material as well as its screen-space shading. Checkpoint: the shading changes while atom counts, connectivity, and element colors stay the same. The automatic radius comes from the atom-coordinate extent, so zooming does not change that radius. The visible effect can still change with the camera. AO emphasizes depth and contact regions by shading atomic spheres and bonds; hidden and offscreen geometry affect what the screen-space method can show. Turn it off if navigation slows. The gallery provides the paired captures for comparison. 3. Switch to chains and protein cartoons Set Ambient occlusion off. Under Molecular data , choose Representation → Protein cartoon , then Biological structure → Coloring → Chain . Use Fit scene to frame the complete complex. Expand Chains . Each row identifies a deposited chain instance. If needed, use Filter chain or entity to find the chain you want; the list displays at most 50 matching entries. For chain A, use Isolate , then Focus . Alternatively, Focus visible structure frames all currently visible atoms. A chain style can override a component style, and either can override the global representation. Choose Coloring → Secondary structure . Inspect deposited helices, strand arrows, and unassigned loops. Click an atom where atomic detail is visible to inspect its biological context. Use Show all components to clear isolation and visibility/range filters. Return to Coloring → Element and Representation → Van der Waals when you want the atomic AO view again. Chain coloring separates the subunits in the complete complex. Protein cartoon geometry has its own diffuse shading; molecular AO applies to atomic spheres and bonds. An isolated chain with deposited secondary-structure coloring. Unknown or unassigned regions remain explicit; EigenVista does not predict secondary structure. Checkpoint: isolation hides other chains without removing them from the document. Missing backbone atoms, chain boundaries, and unsupported gaps break protein paths rather than inventing connections. Nonprotein components retain atomic representations. 4. Export the view and save the data Choose your final representation, colors, and framing. To capture the shaded atomic view, restore Element , Van der Waals , the Pastel palette, and your AO settings first. Use the viewport’s camera button, Export image , for eigenvista-view.png . Or use Export image with transparent background for eigenvista-view-transparent.png . The PNG includes current scene shading and camera framing, without the toolbar or text overlays. Check that your host completed the download. Click Save and choose a new filename such as 1aon-study.eigenvista . This retains the selected molecular data, biological identities, connectivity, and global representation. Keep the original mmCIF file too. Session versus Save: AO, atom palette, background, biological coloring, chain/component style overrides, visibility, isolation, residue ranges, and focus are session settings. They are not written into .eigenvista . Camera framing is also not saved. Reload starts with AO off and the built-in atom palette; load Pastel and restore your display choices to recreate the illustration. A PNG captures the current appearance but is not a molecular document. Image export uses the host’s download mechanism. Browser export is the reference path; native image-download handling still needs qualification. Confirm the PNG arrived before relying on it. If something differs If Pastel seems ineffective, choose Coloring → Element . If an isolated chain vanishes, use Show all components , check chain/component filters, and focus again. If AO reports an enhancement error, disable and re-enable it to retry; normal molecular rendering remains available. A lost graphics context requires a reload, so Save completed work first when possible. Continue in the biological structure reference for component styles and residue ranges, or the scene reference for palettes, backgrounds, and PNG export. Return to the learning path to explore calculated fields.

title: Shape the light
description: Give molecular surfaces an X-ray finish, reveal their interior with clipping, and adjust custom shader parameters live in EigenVista.
text: Reveal the molecular framework through an X-ray shell. Cut into a density surface. Change the lighting, color and transparency while you explore. X-RAY / VIEW-ANGLE OPACITY GLSL SURFACE SHADER The X-ray shader emphasizes the surface silhouette while letting the molecular framework show through. CLIPPING / LOOK INSIDE LIVE PARAMETERS Move a clipping boundary to reveal the structure beneath the surface. The molecular model stays in place. Try it yourself Prepare a surface Give it an X-ray finish Cut into the surface Tune the view live Keep the result Download the presets Start with a molecular surface Custom shaders give you direct control over how an isosurface is drawn. Load a ready-made preset to get started, or bring your own vertex and fragment GLSL files. EigenVista turns their parameters into editable controls in the Surface shader panel. Open bicyclic-c7h10.molden and select its total density under Quantum fields → Density matrices . Set Isovalue to 0.04 electrons/bohr³ and Grid resolution to 256³ , then click Generate surfaces . The images here use this same density mesh. Under Field rendering → Mode , select Isosurface mesh . Use Ball and stick to see the atomic framework alongside it. Frame the molecule with the rotate, zoom and Fit scene controls. For the complete field workflow, see the orbital tutorial . The shaders below work on the generated surface, so you can try several finishes on the same geometry. Give it an X-ray finish This preset makes front-facing areas more transparent and keeps the outline stronger. It is useful when a surface would otherwise hide the atoms inside. Download x-ray.vert , x-ray.frag and x-ray.params . Expand Surface shader . Use Vertex shader… for x-ray.vert and Fragment shader… for x-ray.frag . Use Parameters file… to load x-ray.params . Leave Shader transparency checked. Choose All surfaces under Apply to , or select an individual surface, then click Apply shader . For the illustrated finish, set maxOpacity to 0.85 , minOpacity to 0 and da to 0.03 . Use the toolbar’s background picker for #17232d . Rotate the molecule and adjust color to suit your view. Control What to try color Choose the tint of the shell. minOpacity Raise it to give front-facing areas more body; lower it to see more of the framework. maxOpacity Lower it to soften the strongest edges. da Raise this cutoff to remove the faintest parts of the shell and emphasize its contours. Keep minOpacity at or below maxOpacity . The preset’s eyePosition values start at zero; leave them there for the standard view. Cut into the surface Clipping opens a window into a molecular envelope. Six controls bound a visible box; move one boundary across the molecule to expose what it encloses. Click Clear shader before switching presets. Load surface-clip.vert , surface-clip.frag and surface-clip.params with the same three file buttons. Choose the target under Apply to and click Apply shader . Adjust xmin and xmax , ymin and ymax , or zmin and zmax . Keep each minimum below its matching maximum. Enlarge the bounds first if the surface is mostly hidden. For the illustrated cutaway, keep factor at 0.24 , set all bounds to −10 / 10 , then bring zmax to 0.25 . Set the surface’s Positive color to #93e8d9 . Rotate the view to inspect the exposed framework. The factor control scales the coordinates used by the clipping box. Its preset value is 0.24 ; leave it fixed while finding the six bounds for your molecule. For a solid finish, uncheck Shader transparency . Tune the view live The parameter names come directly from the shader. Numbers, checkboxes, vector components and color pickers appear as appropriate. Once a shader is applied, editing these controls updates the scene immediately: there is no need to generate the surface again. Adjust the finish while keeping the same molecular surface. See the complete workspace . Open the controls at full size . To switch the underlying shape, choose another field or isovalue and generate its surface. To change only the appearance, keep the geometry and adjust the shader. Clear shader returns to the built-in Diffuse or Blinn-Phong surface shading. Keep the result Use Save to keep the molecular data and generated mesh in an .eigenvista document. Click Save parameters in the shader panel to download your current settings as a .params file. Keep it with the vertex and fragment files; load all three to restore the finish in a later session. Use Export image for the current view, or Export image with transparent background to place it on a slide or figure. The molecular document stores the surface geometry; the shader files and saved parameters keep the appearance. See saving and sharing for the document details. More lighting and clipping examples are included in the application package’s Shaders/ folder. For accepted shader files, parameter handling and error messages, see the surface-shader reference . title: About EigenVista
description: A local molecular and quantum-chemistry viewer: design, limitations, data credits and project links.
text: The purpose Local by design Current boundaries Credits The project A viewer for molecular data EigenVista brings atomic structures, imported orbitals, density data and sampled scalar fields into one interactive scene. It is the standalone successor to the Rust Molekel preview. It reads older .molekel preview documents, while new documents use .eigenvista. The aim is to help you inspect supplied scientific data and prepare useful views of it. Local by design The desktop application reads and processes local files on your computer. Its scientific core is written in Rust; the interface uses React and Three.js/WebGL2, inside a Tauri desktop shell. Scientific field work runs in a background WebAssembly worker, keeping progress and cancellation available. There is no calculation server or account required for local molecular-file workflows. This website provides documentation, examples and downloads; it does not upload or analyze your calculation files. A native document can hold structure, supplied quantum data, sampled fields and generated meshes together. Display choices such as the background, palette and AO remain session preferences. See the file reference for what is saved. Know what a view means Imported fields retain their declared meaning. Unknown cube units or scalar meaning are not guessed. Protein secondary structure uses deposited annotations. AO uses screen-space shading to emphasize depth and contact regions. Display bonds are inferred or taken from supported declarations. They do not establish bond order, crystallographic symmetry or a complete chemical interpretation. Version 0.7.2 is an experimental development preview. The downloadable package targets Apple Silicon Macs; Linux, Windows, Intel Mac and the full deployment-OS range are not qualified distributions. Preserve original calculation files and inspect import reports. Images, examples and palettes The molecular images were captured in EigenVista from the repository's public test inputs. The large-structure studies use PDB 1AON and PDB 4PJ1 . See each RCSB entry for the deposited structure and its original scientific citation. The quantum and shader studies use the C₇H₁₀ Molden example , originally distributed with Molekel . See the dataset notes for the source and orbital information. The 29-atom cube study uses complex-field.cube , originally elf_pic.cube in the same Molekel example collection. The small water Molden example remains available as a separate RHF/cc-pVDZ input. Water PDB/XYZ coordinates and the signed-affine cube are demonstration fixtures; the cube is a mathematical signed field, not a quantum calculation. Example sources and notices and the capture record preserve provenance and settings. MatterViz Muted and Pastel are adaptations of Janosh Riebesell's MatterViz element colors . Original RGB values for elements 1–109 are retained; remaining elements use EigenVista defaults. The MIT notice accompanies both palettes. Download Pastel for the recommended AO workflow. The website follows the brutalist laboratory-manual style of the related Sesmesh project . Open project, practical feedback EigenVista is available under GPL-2.0-or-later . Source, release history and issue tracking are on GitHub . Keep license notices and sources with redistributed tester packages. When reporting a problem, include the app version, platform, input format and exact steps. Share only files you have permission to publish. Open an issue ↗
